title: Khadijah: A Remarkable Woman
subtitle: Lineage, Marriage, and the Blessed Household
summary: The noble standing and virtue of Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, her title Al-Tahirah, the marriage proposal through Nafisah bint Munabbih, the reported wedding address, the differing reports of Khadijah's age, the birth of their children, and her enduring place in the Prophet's heart.

sections.text: The Nobility and Character of Khadijah

In the aristocracy of pre-Islamic Makkah, few figures commanded greater respect than Khadijah bint Khuwaylid ibn Asad ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn Qusayy. Belonging to the esteemed clan of Banu Asad, she combined noble lineage with keen intelligence, financial independence, and exceptional moral rectitude. In an era characterized by tribal license and laxity, her reputation for chastity was so renowned that the people of Makkah referred to her by the title Al-Tahirah (The Pure One).

Khadijah had been married twice before, to 'Atiq ibn 'A'idh al-Makhzumi and to Abu Halah al-Tamimi; the sources differ on the order of these marriages. Biographers relate that she had declined proposals from men of standing among Quraysh.
The timeless stone architecture and tranquil quarters of ancient Makkah.
The Marriage Proposal and Familial Agreement

Following the return of the Syrian trade caravan and Maysarah's account, Khadijah resolved to marry Muhammad. According to a report in Ibn Sa'd's Tabaqat, she confided this to her friend Nafisah bint Munabbih, who approached Muhammad discreetly to ask why he had not yet married.

When Muhammad explained that his modest financial means did not allow him to establish a household, Nafisah asked if he would consider a proposal if means, beauty, noble lineage, and character were presented to him in Khadijah bint Khuwaylid. Recognizing her peerless standing and moral dignity, Muhammad welcomed the prospect and consulted his guardians, Abu Talib and Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib.

The formal proposal proceeded in accordance with ancient Arabian nobility. Abu Talib and Hamzah led a delegation of Banu Hashim to the home of Khadijah's family, where they were received by her uncle, 'Amr ibn Asad ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza (her father Khuwaylid having passed away years earlier, according to the predominant historical reports, though some classical narrations mention him as being present).
The Wedding Address of Abu Talib

Later sirah works record a wedding address attributed to Abu Talib. In it he praises God for making them descendants of Ibrahim and Isma'il and custodians of the sacred House, then says of his nephew that, though he has little wealth, no man of Quraysh can be weighed against him without Muhammad outweighing him in nobility and virtue. The source and chain of this address have not been established, and it needs verification before being relied upon.

"No man of Quraysh can be weighed against him without his outweighing him in nobility, virtue and intellect; and if he has little wealth, wealth is a passing shadow and a loan that is reclaimed." — Address attributed to Abu Talib in later sirah works; source unverified

Ibn Hisham records that the dowry was twenty young she-camels. Most accounts state that Muhammad was twenty-five at the time of the marriage. As for Khadijah's age, the best-known report says she was forty, while other reports collected by Ibn Sa'd and others give twenty-eight.
A Blessed Family Life and Children

God blessed their marriage with several children. Their sons were al-Qasim, from whom the Prophet took his kunya Abu al-Qasim, and 'Abdullah, also called al-Tahir and al-Tayyib (some reports treat these as the names of separate sons). Both died in early childhood.

They also had four daughters who survived into adulthood and embraced Islam: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah. The household also included Zayd ibn Harithah, a captured youth whom Khadijah gave to Muhammad. According to the sirah reports, when Zayd's family came to Makkah to ransom him, he chose to remain with Muhammad, who then freed him and adopted him.

Ibn Ishaq relates that during a year of hardship in Makkah, Muhammad took his young cousin 'Ali ibn Abi Talib into his household to ease the burden on Abu Talib, while al-'Abbas took Ja'far. 'Ali thus grew up under Muhammad's care.
The peaceful domestic quarters of Makkah where the Prophet and Khadijah established their blessed home.

For about twenty-five years, until Khadijah's death in the tenth year of prophethood according to most reports, Muhammad took no other wife. In Sahih Muslim, 'A'ishah relates that she was never as jealous of any woman as she was of Khadijah, though Khadijah had died three years before she married the Prophet, because he mentioned her so often; that his Lord commanded him to give Khadijah glad tidings of a house of reed in Paradise; and that when he slaughtered a sheep he would send portions to Khadijah's friends. In a narration in Musnad Ahmad he said of her: 'She believed in me when people disbelieved in me, she affirmed my truth when people called me a liar, she supported me with her wealth when people deprived me, and God granted me children by her.'
